Inside, the passengers see the flash and hear the thunder, but nothing happens to them.\n\nIt is not because of the rubber wheels: lightning has just crossed kilometres of air, and a few centimetres of rubber do not stop it. If there were an electric field inside, it would push them until there was none: in equilibrium, $E = 0$ throughout the metal.\n\nTake Gauss's theorem on a surface inside the metal that surrounds the cavity: since $E = 0$ over all of it, the flux is 0 and it encloses no charge, $Q_{int} = ε_0 ∮ E · dS = 0$. All the charge stays on the outer surface, and in the cavity, if there are no charges inside, there is no field either.

La corriente del rayo busca el camino de: The lightning current looks for the path of least resistance to the ground: the sheet metal of the car, a much better conductor than air or a person. It runs along the outside of the bodywork and jumps to the ground from the underside, next to the wheels.\n\nAircraft are struck by lightning often and keep flying: the current enters at one tip, runs along the outside of the fuselage and leaves through the tail. Inside, only the flash is seen.
